absent: Autogroup allocation, reference counting, task lookup, default group identity, thread iteration, and thread migration mechanics beyond the call sites shown.
Task signal lock structure, signal and task structure layouts, cgroup attachment interaction, and exiting-thread cleanup details.
Weight table contents, load averaging, hierarchy traversal, runqueue layout, group share calculation indirection, and per-entity scheduling state.
Hardware clock source, per-CPU data placement, tick dependency tracking, irqtime accounting, generic clock initialization, and watchdog coordination.
Wakeup state matching, runnable determination, CPU selection, queueing versus direct enqueue, blocking and migration accounting, tracing, and statistics.
Nice resource-limit conversion, capability evaluation, security hook for setting nice, and error code semantics.
Completion and simple-wait queue layouts, task state encodings, wake flag meanings, and preemption guard behavior.
Boot option registration and the runtime effect of disabling automatic grouping on scheduling decisions.

findings.text: The scheduler provides lifecycle handling for automatic task grouping, covering creation with immediate attachment to a task, return of a task to the shared default grouping, inheritance of the current grouping by a new signal owner at fork, and release of the grouping reference when the signal owner exits. Relocation associates the whole thread group with the new grouping while managing references on old and new owners.

Relocation of a process between automatic groups is serialized through the task signal handling lock held across the association swap and the migration of member threads. When the requested grouping already matches the current one no migration occurs. The previous grouping reference is dropped after the serialization is released.

An administrative control allows adjusting the nice level of the automatic group containing a given task, alongside read-only reporting of group identity and nice level and rendering of a filesystem path for group accounting. Reporting and path rendering apply only when the underlying scheduling group is an automatic group; otherwise they produce no output.

Nice adjustment on an automatic group uses exclusive access to the group while updating shares and the stored nice value, while status display uses shared access. Share updates are further serialized by a dedicated shares mutex owned by the fair scheduling logic.

Several facilities have build-dependent dual forms. Idle-group detection either tests a counter or always reports non-idle; load scaling either shifts by a fixed-point amount or acts as identity; fair-group refresh either recomputes weight or does nothing; autogroup membership either tests a back-pointer or always reports false; share setting either performs hierarchy work or reports success immediately; and autogroup helpers collapse to no-ops when disabled.

Fair scheduling exposes control of aggregate group weight. The outer operation validates the target and delegates to an inner routine that stores the new weight and refreshes accounting on every possible processor, walking upward through nested scheduling entities to update averages and group contributions.

Group weight changes require holding the shares mutex, asserted by the inner routine. Per-processor propagation takes each runqueue lock with interrupts saved, refreshes the runqueue clock, and releases in reverse order. Runqueue lock and unlock primitives pair pinning with raw spin acquisition and interrupt state save and restore.

Weight updates are rejected for the idle group and for the root group. Requested values are clamped into a scheduler-defined minimum to maximum interval before comparison, and an unchanged effective value completes without further work.

An automatic group descriptor combines lifetime tracking with scheduling linkage and administrative state. It holds a reference count, an association to a scheduling group, a reader-writer semaphore guarding administrative updates, a numeric identity, and a stored nice level. The count reflects potential users rather than currently attached threads.

Per-processor scheduler clock tracking keeps three timestamps covering raw hardware readings, wall-clock readings, and the derived scheduler time. Global state adds an offset aligning hardware time to scheduler time, a wall-clock adjustment, running and stable indicators, and an early-boot stability assumption.

Scheduler clock stability moves between unstable and stable under boot and runtime events. Early boot assumes stability, initial setup aligns offsets with interrupts disabled and marks running, late setup either confirms stability or disables irqtime accounting. A stable marking computes a continuity offset and clears a tick dependency, while detection of instability schedules asynchronous work that snapshots time, replicates it to all processors, disables irqtime accounting, and marks unstable.

Time services include non-instrumented and preempt-guarded local clock readers, a weak running-clock alias, periodic tick maintenance for stable and unstable modes, and idle sleep and wakeup hooks. The periodic tick and wakeup paths are inert when stable, when the clock is not marked running, or when timekeeping is suspended.

Local time selection prefers hardware time plus a global offset when marked stable, falls back to raw hardware time when not yet running, and otherwise uses per-processor tracking state. Stable ticks only refresh the wall-clock adjustment under protection, while unstable ticks snapshot both time bases and advance per-processor state with interrupts already disabled.

Nice permission distinguishes lowering from raising priority by converting the requested nice value to a resource-limit scale and comparing against the target limit, succeeding when the conversion shows a reduction or when the caller holds the relevant system privilege.

Wakeup and placement services attempt to make a sleeping task runnable and to assign a task to a processor. Wakeup reports whether the task state matched and accounts success statistically, while placement updates migration statistics and notifies tracing and performance subsystems when the processor changes, invoking class-specific relocation hooks when present.

Remote wakeup holds the task priority-inheritance lock with interrupts saved across state matching and queueing decisions. Changing a task processor requires holding either that same lock for waking tasks or the associated runqueue lock for runnable tasks, with group moves holding both to pin the scheduling group.

Waking the currently running task uses a lock-free fast path that clears blocking state and performs the wakeup directly. Other tasks undergo ordered checks of state, queue membership, processor residency, and placement, transitioning through a waking state to allow lock release before enqueue, with special handling for migration, I/O wait accounting, and proxy execution fixups.

Several misuses trigger one-time warnings or degraded behavior, including waking the current task while marked delayed or blocked, reweighting an entity against an unexpected queue, assigning blocked or offline processors or violating migration-disabled constraints, and marking an unstable clock after boot with a firmware warning. Unprivileged nice changes on automatic groups are rate limited and treated as a heavyweight global operation.

Completion signaling increments a done counter unless already saturated and then wakes waiters under the wait queue lock. Simple-wait wakeup only acts when the queue is non-empty, waking the oldest waiter and removing it from the list.

Load weight maintenance adjusts an aggregate counter and invalidates a cached reciprocal. Entity reweighting preserves queue accounting by detaching averages, installing the new weight, refreshing derived load figures, reattaching averages, and updating queue totals only when the entity is queued, skipping work when the weight is unchanged and preserving empty-group weight for deferred dequeue handling.
A boot-time option disables automatic grouping by clearing the corresponding enable control and reporting successful handling.
The automatic grouping header uses a standard multiple-inclusion guard to ensure its declarations are processed once per translation unit.

Administrative and weight facts: requested autogroup nice values are validated against scheduler minimum and maximum nice bounds; the nice to weight conversion uses a forty-entry table with an offset of twenty; unprivileged changes are throttled to one per tenth of a timer second; and group weights are clamped between scheduler minimum and maximum share bounds after fixed-point scaling.

Completion saturation occurs at the maximum unsigned integer value rather than wrapping. Automatic group display and path facts combine a fixed label with the numeric group identity and, for display, the stored nice level, emitted only for genuine automatic groups.
